Now make a bargain with my master, the king of Assyria. I will give you two thousand horses if you have riders to mount them.
How can you turn back even one of the least of my master's officers, when you rely on Egypt to give you chariots and horsemen?
And now, do you suppose that I have marched against this land to destroy it without the Lord? The Lord himself told me, ‘March against this land and destroy it.’”

Eliakim son of Hilkiah, Shebna, and Joah said to the chief cupbearer, “Please speak to your servants in Aramaic, because we understand it. Do not speak to us in Judean in the hearing of the people standing on the wall.”

The chief cupbearer said to them, “My master did not send me to you and your master to say these things, but to the men sitting on the wall, so that they will not have to eat their own excrement and drink their own urine along with you.”
The chief cupbearer stood and called out loudly in Judean, saying, “Hear the words of the great king, the king of Assyria!
This is what the king says: Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, because he cannot rescue you from my hands.
Do not let Hezekiah make you rely on the Lord by saying, ‘The Lord will certainly rescue us, and this city will not be handed over to the king of Assyria.’

Do not listen to Hezekiah, for this is what the king of Assyria says: Make peace with me and come out to me. Then each of you may eat from his own vines and his own fig trees, and each may drink water from his own cistern,

until I come and take you to a land like your own, a land of grain crops and fruit, a land of grain and vineyards, a land of olives, oil, and honey. Live, and do not die! Do not listen to Hezekiah. Do not let Hezekiah mislead you by saying, ‘The Lord will rescue us.’
Have the gods of the nations been able to rescue their lands, each god his own land, from the hands of the king of Assyria?
Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah? Did they rescue Samaria from my hands?
Which of all the gods of these lands has rescued his land from my hands, that the LORD should rescue Jerusalem from my hands?
The people remained silent and gave him no answer, because the king had commanded, “Do not answer him.”
Eliakim son of Hilkiah, the palace administrator, Shebna the secretary, and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder, came to Hezekiah with their clothes torn and told him what the Rabshakeh had said.
When King Hezekiah heard this, he tore his clothes, covered himself with sackcloth, and entered the house of the Lord.
He sent Eliakim the palace administrator, Shebna the secretary, and the elders of the priests, wearing sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz.
They said to him, “This is what Hezekiah says: Today is a day of distress, rebuke, and wrath. The pains of childbirth have come, but the woman in labor has no strength.”

Perhaps the LORD your God will hear the words of the Rabshakeh, whom his master, the king of Assyria, sent to insult the living God, and will rebuke him for the words that the LORD your God has heard. Offer supplication and prayer for the remnant that is left.
The servants of King Hezekiah came to the prophet Isaiah.
Isaiah said to them, “Tell your master this: This is what the LORD says: Do not be afraid of the words you have heard, with which the messengers of the king of Assyria have blasphemed me.”
Look, I will put a spirit in him, and he will hear news and return to his own land. I will make him fall by the sword in his own land.
The Rabshakeh returned and found the king of Assyria fighting against Libnah, for he had heard that the king had left Lachish.
The king heard that Tirhakah, king of Cush, had come out to fight against him, and he again sent messengers to Hezekiah.
Tell Hezekiah king of Judah this: Do not let your God, in whom you trust, deceive you. You say, “Jerusalem will not be handed over to the king of Assyria.”
You have heard everything the kings of Assyria have done to all the lands, laying them waste. Will you escape?
Did the gods of the nations rescue any of their lands that my fathers destroyed—Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, and the people of Eden who were in Telassar?
Where is the king of Hamath, the king of Arpad, the king of the city of Sepharvaim, or those of Hena and Ivvah?”
Hezekiah took the letters from the messengers and read them. He went up to the house of the LORD, and Hezekiah spread the letters out before the LORD.
Hezekiah prayed before the LORD and said, “LORD Almighty, God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, you alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth. You made heaven and earth.”
Incline your ear, LORD, and hear. Open your eyes, LORD, and see. Hear all the words of Sennacherib, which he sent to insult the living God.
Truly, Lord, the kings of Assyria have devastated all the lands, including their own land.
They burned their gods in the fire, because they were not gods but the work of human hands, made of wood and stone. So they burned them.
Now, LORD our God, save us from his hands, so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the LORD God.
Isaiah son of Amoz sent word to Hezekiah, saying, “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: I have heard everything you prayed before me concerning Sennacherib king of Assyria.”
This is the word the LORD has spoken against him: The virgin daughter of Zion despises you and mocks you. The daughter of Jerusalem shakes her head behind you.
Whom have you insulted, and against whom have you blasphemed? Against whom have you raised your voice? You have lifted your eyes on high against the Holy One of Israel.

Through your messengers you have insulted the LORD and said, “With my many chariots I will climb the mountain heights and the slopes of Lebanon. I will cut down its tall cedars and its choicest cypresses. I will enter its farthest heights, the forest of Carmel.”
I will dig and drink water, and with the hooves of my horses I will dry up all the mighty rivers.’
Have you not heard that I did this long ago and prepared it in ancient days? Now I have brought it about, so that you should become a ruin and a wasteland, like fortified cities.

Their inhabitants had little strength; they were shattered and put to shame. They became like grass in the field, like tender green shoots, like grass on a roof, and like blighted grain before it grows tall.
I know when you sit down, when you come in, and when you go out, and how you have exalted yourself against me.

Because you have acted insolently and exalted yourself against me, and your blasphemy has reached my ears, I will put a ring in your nose and a bridle between your lips, and I will turn you back along the road by which you came.
This will be the sign for you: This year you will eat what grows by itself, and in the second year what springs up from that. In the third year, sow and reap, plant vineyards and eat their fruit.
The surviving remnant of the house of Judah will again put down roots below and bear fruit above.
For a remnant will come out of Jerusalem, and survivors from Mount Zion. The zeal of the LORD Almighty will do this.
Therefore this is what the LORD says concerning the king of Assyria: He will not enter this city or shoot an arrow there. He will not surround it with shields or set ambushes against it.
But he will return by the way he came, and he will not enter this city, says the Lord.
I will defend this city and save it for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David.
That night the angel of the LORD went out and killed one hundred and eighty-five thousand in the Assyrian camp. When people rose early in the morning and looked, there they all were—dead bodies.
They broke camp and departed, and Sennacherib king of Assyria returned and lived in Nineveh.

While he was worshiping in the temple of his god Nisroch, his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer killed him with the sword. They escaped to the land of Ararat, and his son Esarhaddon became king after him.

In those days Hezekiah became mortally ill. The prophet Isaiah son of Amoz came to him and said, “This is what the Lord says: Put your household in order, because you are going to die; you will not live.”
Hezekiah turned his face toward the wall and prayed before the Lord, saying,
“Please, Lord, remember that I have walked before you faithfully and with an undivided heart, and have done what is good in your sight.” And Hezekiah wept bitterly.
Isaiah had not yet gone out into the middle courtyard when the word of the Lord came to him, saying,

“Go back and tell Hezekiah, the leader of my people: This is what the Lord, the God of your ancestor David, says: I have heard your prayer and seen your tears. Look, I am healing you, and on the third day you will go up to the house of the Lord.

I will add fifteen years to your life. I will rescue you and this city from the power of the king of Assyria. I will protect this city and save it for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David.”
Isaiah said, “Let them take a cake of figs and put it on the boil, and he will recover.”
Hezekiah said to Isaiah, “What is the sign that the Lord will heal me and that I will go up to the house of the Lord on the third day?”
Isaiah said, “This is the sign for you from the Lord that the Lord will do what he has said: Should the shadow move forward ten steps, or should it go back ten steps?”
Hezekiah said, “It is a small thing for the shadow to move forward ten steps. No, let the shadow go backward ten steps instead.”
The prophet Isaiah called to the Lord, and he turned the shadow back on the steps, and the sun went backward ten steps on the steps of Ahaz.
At that time Merodach-baladan son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and gifts to Hezekiah, because he had heard that Hezekiah had been ill and had recovered.

Hezekiah was pleased with them and showed them his treasury—the silver, gold, spices, fine oils, his entire armory, and everything found in his treasuries. There was nothing in his palace or anywhere in his realm that Hezekiah did not show them.
The prophet Isaiah came to King Hezekiah and said to him, “What did these men say to you, and where did they come from?” Hezekiah said, “They came to me from a distant land, from Babylon.”
He said, “What did they see in your palace?” Hezekiah said, “They saw everything in my palace. I left nothing in my palace or my treasury that I did not show them.”
Isaiah said to Hezekiah, “Hear the word of the LORD.”

“Look, the days are coming when everything in your palace will be carried away, and the treasure your ancestors have stored up until today will go to Babylon. Nothing will be left to you, says the Lord.
Some of your sons who are born to you, who come from you, will be taken away and will become eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.”
Hezekiah said to Isaiah, “The word of the Lord that you have spoken is good. But let there at least be peace and stability in my days.”

The rest of Hezekiah’s deeds, all his mighty achievements, and how he made the pool and the water channel and brought water into the city are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.
Hezekiah died and rested with his ancestors, and his son Manasseh reigned after him.
Manasseh was twelve years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for fifty-five years. His mother’s name was Hephzibah.
He did what was evil in the LORD’s sight, following the detestable practices of the nations that the LORD had destroyed before the Israelites.
He rebuilt the high places that his father Hezekiah had torn down. He erected an altar to Baal and made idols, as King Ahab of Israel had done. He worshiped all the host of heaven and served them.
He built an altar in the house about which the LORD had said, “In Jerusalem I will place my name.”
He built altars to all the heavenly hosts in the two courtyards of the LORD’s house.
He made his son pass through fire, practiced divination and interpreted omens, and appointed mediums and spiritists. He did much evil in the Lord’s sight, provoking him to anger.

He placed the image of the idol he had made in the house of the Lord, the house about which the Lord had said to David and his son Solomon, “In this house and in Jerusalem, which I chose from all the tribes of Israel, I will place my name forever.
I will no longer make Israel’s feet wander from the land I gave their ancestors, provided they are careful to do everything I commanded them and to keep all the laws my servant Moses commanded them.”
But they did not listen. Manasseh led them astray and did worse than the nations the Lord had destroyed before the Israelites.
The LORD spoke through his servants the prophets:
“Because Manasseh son of Hezekiah, king of Judah, has done these deeds and has done worse than everything the Amorites before him did, and has caused Judah to sin with his idols,
therefore this is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says: Look, I am bringing disaster on Judah and Jerusalem, so that both ears of everyone who hears of it will ring.

I will stretch over Jerusalem the measuring line of Samaria and the plumb line of the house of Ahab. I will wipe Jerusalem away and destroy it because of all the impurity that Manasseh practiced in Judah.
I will abandon the remnant of my inheritance and hand them over to their enemies. They will become plunder and be trampled by all their enemies.
For they have done evil before me and have provoked me to anger from the day their ancestors came out of Egypt until today.
Manasseh also shed a very great amount of innocent blood, until he filled Jerusalem from one end to the other, besides the sins by which he caused Judah to sin and do what was evil before the Lord.
The rest of the acts of Manasseh, everything he did, and the sins he committed are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.
Manasseh died and joined his ancestors. He was buried in the garden of his house, in the garden of Gaza. His son Amon succeeded him as king.
Amon was twenty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for two years. His mother's name was Meshullemeth, daughter of Haduz, from Jotbah.
He did what was evil in the LORD’s sight, as his father Manasseh had done.
He followed all the ways of his father, served the idols his father had served, and bowed down to them.
He abandoned the LORD, the God of his ancestors, and did not follow the LORD’s way.
Amon’s servants rebelled against him and killed him in his house.
The people of the land killed everyone who had rebelled against King Amon, and the people of the land made his son Josiah king in his place.
The rest of the acts of Amon and everything he did are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.
They buried him in his tomb in the garden of Gaza, and his son Josiah became king after him.
Josiah was eight years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for thirty-one years. His mother's name was Jedidah, daughter of Azariah, from Bozkath.
He did what was right before the Lord and followed the entire path that his ancestor David had followed. He did not turn aside to the right or to the left.
In the eighteenth year of King Josiah, the king sent Shaphan the scribe, son of Azaliah, son of Meshullam, to the house of the Lord, saying:
“Go up to Hilkiah the high priest, and have him hand over the money brought into the house of the Lord, which the doorkeepers have collected from the people.
Let them hand it over to the workers in the house of the Lord to repair the damage to the house of the Lord.
Let them hand it over to the carpenters, masons, and architects to buy timber and cut stone to strengthen the house of the Lord.
But no accounting was required of them for the money entrusted to them, because they worked faithfully.
Hilkiah the high priest said to Shaphan the scribe, “I have found the Book of the Law in the house of the Lord.” Hilkiah the priest gave the Book of the Law to Shaphan the scribe, and he read it.
Shaphan the scribe came to the king to report to him and said, “Your servants have handed over the money found in the house and have delivered it to the workers appointed over the house of the Lord.”
Shaphan the scribe informed the king, saying, “Hilkiah the priest has given me the Book of the Law.” Then Shaphan read it before the king.
When the king heard the words of the book of the law, he tore his clothes.
The king gave orders to Hilkiah, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Achbor son of Micah, Shaphan the scribe, and Asaiah the king's servant, saying:

“Go and inquire of the Lord for me, for all the people, and for all Judah concerning the words of this book that has been found. For great is the Lord's anger against us, because our ancestors did not obey the words of this book by doing what is written in it.”

Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan, and Asaiah went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum son of Tikvah, son of Harhas, the keeper of the garments. She was living in Jerusalem, in [?], and they spoke with her.
She said to them, “This is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says: Tell the man who sent you to me:
“This is what the Lord says: Look, I am bringing disaster upon this place and its inhabitants—all the words of the book that the king of Judah has read.
Because they have abandoned me and burned incense to other gods, provoking me to anger with the work of their hands, my anger will blaze against this place, says the Lord, and I will destroy you.
But to the king of Judah who sent you to inquire of the Lord, say this: This is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says concerning the words you have heard:

Because your heart was distressed and you trembled before the Lord when you heard what I said against this place and its inhabitants—that they would become an object of horror and a curse—and because you tore your clothes and wept before me, I too have heard you, says the Lord.

Therefore, look, I will gather you to your ancestors, and you will be gathered to your grave in peace. Your eyes will not see any of the disaster that I am bringing upon this place.” They brought the report back to the king.
The king sent word, and all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem gathered before him.

The king went up to the house of the Lord, and all the people of Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem went with him, along with the priests, the prophets, and all the people, from the least to the greatest. He read before them all the words of the book of the covenant that had been found in the house of the Lord.

The king stood by the pillar and made a covenant before the Lord to follow the Lord and keep his commandments, his testimonies, and his statutes with all their heart and all their soul, carrying out the words of this covenant written in this book. All the people joined in the covenant.

The king commanded Hilkiah the high priest, the priests under him, and the gatekeepers to bring out of the house of the Lord all the vessels made for Baal, for the idols, and for all the host of heaven. They burned them outside Jerusalem in the fields [?] of Kidron, and he carried their ashes to Bethel.

He killed the pagan priests whom the kings of Judah had appointed to burn incense at the high places in the towns of Judah and around Jerusalem, as well as those who burned incense to Baal, to the sun, to the moon, to the stars, and to all the host of heaven.

He brought the idol out of the house of the Lord, outside Jerusalem to the Kidron Valley. He burned it in the Kidron Valley, reduced it to dust, and scattered its dust over the graves of the common people.
He tore down the houses of the male prostitutes in the LORD’s house, and those of the women who wove garments for the idols there.

He brought all the priests from the towns of Judah and defiled the high places where the priests had burned incense, from Dan to Beersheba. He tore down the high place at the entrance to the Gate of Deliverance in the town, on a man's left.
However, the priests of the high places did not go up to the altar of the Lord in Jerusalem, but they did eat unleavened bread with their fellow priests.
He tore down the high places that the kings of Judah had made at Topheth in the Valley of Ben Hinnom for a person to make his son or daughter pass through the fire to Molech.

They killed the horses that the kings of Judah had dedicated to the sun at the entrance to the house of the Lord, at the treasury of Nathan, the king's eunuch, in the adjoining precinct. He burned the chariot of the sun with fire.

The king tore down the altar on the roof of Ahaz's upper room, which the kings of Judah had made, and the altars that Manasseh had made in the two courtyards of the house of the Lord. He ran from there and threw their dust into the Kidron Valley.

King Josiah tore down the high places east of Jerusalem, south of the Mount of Destruction, which Solomon king of Israel had built for Ashtoreth, the goddess of the Sidonians, for Chemosh, the idol of Moab, and for Milcom, the idol of the Ammonites.
He broke the sacred pillars, cut down the idols, and filled their sites with human bones.

He also tore down the altar at Bethel and the high places that Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin, had made. He tore down that altar and the high place, burned the high place, crushed it to dust, and burned the idols.

Josiah turned and saw graves there on the hill. He sent men to take bones from the graves, burned them on the altar, and defiled it, according to the word of the Lord spoken by the prophet of God who had proclaimed these things.

The king said, "What is this monument I see?" The men of the town told him, "It is the grave of the prophet of God who came from Judah and proclaimed these things that you have done to the altar at Bethel."
He said, "Leave him alone. Let no one approach the grave, and let no one disturb his bones." So they left his bones undisturbed, along with the bones of the prophet who had come from Samaria.
Josiah also removed all the shrines at the high places in the towns of Samaria that the kings of Israel had made to provoke the Lord to anger. He did to them what he had done at Bethel.
He slaughtered all the pagan priests of the high places who had burned incense on the altars, and he burned human bones on them. Then he returned to Jerusalem.
The king commanded all the people, saying, "Celebrate the Passover to the Lord your God, as it is written in this book of the covenant."
For no Passover like this had been celebrated since the days of the judges who judged Israel, throughout all the days of the kings of Israel and the kings of Judah.
Only in the eighteenth year of King Josiah was this Passover celebrated to the LORD in Jerusalem.

Josiah also eradicated the mediums, the spiritists, the images, the idols, and all the abominations that were seen in the land of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem, in order to carry out the words of the book of the law written in the book that Hilkiah the priest had found in the house of the Lord.

Before him there had been no king like him who turned to the Lord with all his heart, all his soul, and all his strength, according to what is written in the law of Moses. Nor did anyone like him arise after him.
Nevertheless, the LORD did not turn from his great anger that burned against Judah because of the anger Manasseh had provoked in him.
The Lord said, "I will also remove Judah from my presence, just as I removed Israel. I will reject this city that I chose, Jerusalem, and the house of which I said, 'My name will be there.'"
The rest of the acts of Josiah, and everything he did, are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.

In his days, Pharaoh the Lame, king of Egypt, marched against Mabbug on the Euphrates River. King Josiah went out to meet him in battle. Pharaoh said to him, “I am not coming against you. Stay out of my way.” But Josiah would not listen to him, and Pharaoh struck him down and killed him at Megiddo when he saw him there.

His servants carried him away dead from Megiddo, brought him to Jerusalem, and buried him there in his tomb. The people of the land took Jehoahaz son of Josiah, anointed him, and made him king in place of his father.
Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for three months. His mother’s name was Hamutal, daughter of Jeremiah from Libnah.
He did what was evil before the LORD, just as Manasseh had done.

Pharaoh the Lame, king of Egypt, imprisoned him at Diblath in the land of Hamath while he was reigning in Jerusalem. He imposed a tribute on the land of one hundred talents of silver and ten talents of gold.
Pharaoh the Lame made Eliakim son of Josiah king in place of his father Josiah and changed his name to Jehoiakim. He took Jehoahaz away, and Jehoahaz went to Egypt and died there.

Jehoiakim gave the silver and gold to Pharaoh, but he imposed a levy of silver and gold on the land according to Pharaoh’s command. Each person among the people of the land brought silver and gold according to his assessment, as Pharaoh the Lame had commanded.
Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for eleven years. His mother’s name was Zebidah, daughter of Peraiah from Ramah.
He did what was evil in the LORD’s sight, as his ancestors had done.
In his days, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon marched against Jerusalem. Jehoiakim became his servant for three years, but then turned against him and rebelled.

The Lord sent raiding bands of Chaldeans, Edomites, Moabites, and Ammonites against him. He sent them against Judah to destroy them, according to the word of the Lord that he had spoken through his servants the prophets.
At the Lord’s command, great wrath came upon Judah to remove them from his presence because of the sins of Manasseh and everything he had done.
and because of the innocent blood he had shed, filling Jerusalem with innocent blood. The LORD was unwilling to forgive.
The rest of Jehoiakim’s deeds and everything he did are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.
Jehoiakim rested with his ancestors, and his son Jehoiachin became king after him.
The king of Egypt did not come out of his land again, because the king of Babylon had taken everything that belonged to the king of Egypt, from the Brook of Egypt to the Euphrates River.
Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for three months. His mother’s name was Nehushta, daughter of Eliathan from Jerusalem.
He did what was evil in the LORD’s sight, as his father had done.
At that time Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up against Jerusalem, and the city was besieged.
King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon came against the land while his servants were besieging the city.

Jehoiachin king of Judah went out to the king of Babylon, together with his mother, his servants, his officials, and his eunuchs. The king of Babylon took him away with him in the eighth year of his reign.

He carried away from there all the treasure of the Lord’s house and the treasure of the king’s palace. He cut up all the gold vessels that Solomon king of Israel had made for the Lord’s house, just as the Lord had said.
He deported all Jerusalem, all the officials, and all the mighty warriors—ten thousand captives—as well as all the smiths and runners. He left no one except the poor among the people of the land.
He deported Jehoiachin to Babylon, along with the king’s mother, the king’s wives, his eunuchs, and the nobles of the land. He took them into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon.
The king of Babylon brought all the strong men—seven thousand—and the smiths and runners—one thousand—into exile in Babylon, all of them men fit for battle.
The king of Babylon made Mattaniah, Jehoiachin’s uncle, king in his place and changed his name to Zedekiah.
Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for eleven years. His mother’s name was Hamutal, daughter of Jeremiah from Libnah.
He did what was evil in the LORD’s sight, as Jehoiakim had done.
The Lord’s anger was against Judah and Jerusalem until he cast them out of his presence. Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.

In the ninth year of his reign, on the tenth day of the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came against Jerusalem with his whole army. He encamped against it and built siegeworks all around it.
The city remained under siege until the eleventh year of King Zedekiah.
In the eleventh year of King Zedekiah, on the ninth day of the fifth month, the famine became severe in the city, and there was no bread for the people of the land.

The city wall was breached, and all the fighting men fled. They left the city at night by way of the gate between the walls beside the king’s garden, while the Chaldeans surrounded the city. They went along the road toward the plain.
The Chaldean army pursued the king and overtook him in the plain of Jericho. His entire army scattered away from him.
They captured the king and brought him up to the king of Babylon at Diblah, and he pronounced judgment on him.
The king of Babylon slaughtered King Zedekiah’s sons before his eyes. He blinded Zedekiah, bound him in chains, and took him to Babylon.

In the fifth month, on the ninth day of the month, in the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, a servant of the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem.
He burned the house of the Lord, the king’s palace, and all the houses of Jerusalem. He burned all the houses of the leading men with fire.
The entire Chaldean army accompanying the captain of the guard tore down the wall all around Jerusalem.

Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, deported the rest of the people who remained in the city, the deserters who had gone over to the king of Babylon, and the remainder of the army, and took them to Babylon.
Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, left some of the poor people of the land to tend vineyards and cultivate the fields.
The Chaldeans broke up the bronze pillars in the house of the Lord, the basins, and the bronze Sea in the house of the Lord. They took all their bronze and carried it to Babylon.
They took the pots, shovels, buckets, spoons, and all the bronze utensils used in the service.
The captain of the guard also took the censers, the gold and silver bowls, and the cups.
The two pillars, the one Sea, and the basins that King Solomon had made for the house of the Lord—the bronze of these objects was beyond weighing.

As for those pillars, each pillar was eighteen cubits high, with a bronze capital on top. The capital was three cubits high, with rings and pomegranates all around the capital, all of bronze. The other pillar was the same, and all of it was bronze.
The captain of the guard took Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the priest who ranked next to him, and the three gatekeepers.

From the city he took one eunuch who was in charge of the fighting men, five men who attended the king and were found in the city, the scribe and the army commander who recruited the people of the land, and sixty men from the people of the land who remained in the city.
Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, took them and brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah.
The king of Babylon struck them down and killed them at Riblah in the land of Hamath. He deported Judah from its land.
Over the people who remained in the land of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had left there, he appointed Gedaliah son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan.

All the army commanders and their men heard that the king of Babylon had put Gedaliah in authority. They came to Gedaliah at Mizpah: Ishmael son of Nethaniah, Johanan son of Kareah, Seraiah son of Tanhumeth, Tobiah, and Jaazaniah son of Maacah, together with their men.
Gedaliah swore an oath to them and their men and said to them, “Do not be afraid of the Chaldeans. Stay in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and things will go well for you.”

In the seventh month, Ishmael son of Nethaniah, son of Ishmael, who was of royal descent, came with ten men. They struck Gedaliah, and he died. They also struck down the Jews and the Chaldeans who were with him at Mizpah.
All the people of the land, from the least to the greatest, and all the army commanders set out and went to Egypt, because they were afraid of the Chaldeans.

In the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in the twelfth month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, Evil-merodach king of Babylon, in the first year of his reign, restored Jehoiachin king of Judah to favor and brought him out of prison.
He spoke kindly to him and placed his throne above the thrones of the other kings who were with him in Babylon.
He changed out of his prison clothes and ate regularly in the king’s presence all the days of his life.
As for his allowance, a regular allowance was given to him by the king of Babylon every day, for all the days of his life.
